$comment: Link-integrity policy for `npm run docs:links` (markdown-link-check 3.15.0).
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
The link gate reads URLs out of repository Markdown, which is untrusted input:
any branch, patch or pull request can put an arbitrary URL in a documentation
page. Without this policy the checker dereferences every one of those URLs from
whichever machine runs the gate - a reviewer's workstation or a CI runner. It
issues a HEAD, falls back to a GET, follows up to eight redirects, resolves DNS
for the host, reads absolute `file:` targets off the local disk, and performs an
MX lookup for `mailto:` addresses. That is a server-side request forgery sink
(CWE-918): a link such as `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` turns the
gate into an internal-network and local-file oracle, and can trigger side
effects on internal GET endpoints.
WHY A DENYLIST IS NOT THE FIX
Filtering which hosts are allowed still leaves the request being made, so the
filter is bypassable by an HTTP redirect to an internal address or by DNS
rebinding. markdown-link-check cannot be told to stop following redirects - its
CLI copies only ignorePatterns, replacementPatterns, httpHeaders, timeout,
ignoreDisable, retryOn429, retryCount, fallbackRetryDelay, aliveStatusCodes and
reporters out of this file, and `maxRedirects` is not among them.
WHAT THIS POLICY DOES INSTEAD - IT REMOVES THE SINK
The gate is made hermetic: it performs no network I/O at all, so there is no
request to forge, no redirect to follow and no name to resolve. Every extracted
link takes exactly one of three paths:
1. `http:`, `https:` and `mailto:` links are matched by `ignorePatterns`, which
markdown-link-check evaluates BEFORE it calls the checker, short-circuiting
with status `ignored`. No HEAD, no GET, no redirect, no DNS or MX lookup.
2. Every other absolute target - including absolute `file:` URLs, scheme-
relative `//host/...` URLs, opaque schemes such as `javascript:` and
`data:`, and paths that traverse above the repository root - is rewritten by
`replacementPatterns` onto a repository-relative path that cannot exist, so
it is reported as a dead link and fails the gate loudly instead of being
fetched or read.
3. Repository-relative links and `#anchor` links are validated the way they
always were: against the filesystem and against the headings of the page
being checked. This is the integrity the gate exists for, because the
documentation set grows from one file to twenty in a single change and
relative-link correctness cannot be assumed.
THE DELIBERATE TRADE-OFF
External links are no longer liveness-checked, because dereferencing untrusted
URLs is precisely the vulnerability. Nothing is lost in practice: this project's
documentation cites source as plain `path:line` text rather than as hyperlinks,
and it deliberately documents a loopback-only service, so `http://127.0.0.1:3000/`
is a legitimate URL to find in its prose. Such a URL is skipped rather than
rejected - it is never dereferenced either way - so honest documentation cannot
be failed by this policy while a smuggled `file:` or `javascript:` target still
is.
Regexes below are written with explicit character classes rather than the `i`
flag, because markdown-link-check compiles each pattern with `new RegExp(pattern)`
and passes no flags: an uppercase `HTTP://` scheme would otherwise slip past a
lowercase-only pattern.
Web links are never dereferenced. Matching here short-circuits the check
before any socket is opened, which is what removes the SSRF sink for the
entire `http`/`https` protocol family - loopback, RFC1918, link-local and
cloud-metadata addresses included. Anchored at the start of the link and
requiring the `:` immediately after the scheme, so a relative path that
merely begins with those letters (for example `httpstuff.md`) is still
checked on the filesystem.
Mail links are never dereferenced either. link-check validates a
`mailto:` address through node-email-verifier with `checkMx: true`, which
performs a live MX DNS lookup for whatever domain the Markdown supplies.
That is the same untrusted-input-to-network-egress problem as an HTTP
fetch, so it is short-circuited the same way.
Any remaining absolute URL that carries an authority - notably
`file:///etc/passwd`, but also `ftp:`, `ws:` and anything else - is
rewritten onto a repository-relative path that does not exist. The
checker then resolves it with `fs.access` inside the directory of the
page being checked, reports HTTP 400, and the gate exits non-zero. The
hostile target is never opened, and the failure is visible rather than
silently skipped. The sentinel begins with `./`, so it can never be
re-matched by a later pattern in this list.
Scheme-relative URLs such as `//169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`.
These carry no scheme of their own, so they escape the `ignorePatterns`
above, and resolving one against a `file:` base yields a URL with a
non-local host that the checker cannot convert to a path. Rejecting them
outright is both safer and clearer than letting that happen.
Opaque absolute targets - `javascript:`, `data:`, `tel:`, a Windows
drive letter such as `C:/...`, or any other scheme without an authority.
None of these belongs in documentation, and none can be resolved as a
repository-relative link, so they are rejected. `mailto:` never reaches
this pattern because it is ignored above, and a relative path is never
caught because the pattern is anchored on a leading letter, so `./a:b.md`
passes through untouched.
Relative paths that climb above the repository root, which would let a
documentation change read arbitrary files on the machine running the
gate - the same local-file oracle as an absolute `file:` URL, just
spelled relatively. Three or more consecutive `../` segments are always
an escape: the deepest authored page sits two directories below the root
(docs/<section>/<page>.md), so `../../` already reaches the root and is
left working. Legitimate links such as `../../README.md` are therefore
unaffected.

$comment-retry: Availability control (CWE-400). link-check reads the `Retry-After` header of a
429 response, multiplies it by 1000 and hands it straight to `setTimeout` with
no upper bound, so a single controlled link answering
`429 Retry-After: 31536000` would stall the gate for a year - twice over, since
it retries. Setting `retryOn429` to false makes that branch unreachable: it is
the first term of the guard around the retry. This file is loaded after the
command line is parsed, so the value here also overrides a `-r`/`--retry` flag
if one is ever reintroduced into the `docs:links` script.
`timeout` bounds each individual check. With the policy above no request is
issued at all, so it is a backstop rather than the primary control, and it
keeps the gate bounded if a future change ever re-enables a network protocol.
